verdicts.evidence: All four target pages exist in the repo: concepts/packages/_index.md ("title: Pulumi packages"), concepts/components/_index.md ("title: Components"), packaging-components.md, and publishing-packages.md. packaging-components.md has the headings "## Source-based plugin packages" (L44) and "## Executable-based plugin packages" (L73), so the #source-based-plugin-packages and #executable-based-plugin-packages anchors resolve.

verdicts.text: Pulumi packages come in two flavors (source-based and executable-based), and each is versioned and released differently.
verdicts.evidence: The sibling page packaging-components.md splits plugin Pulumi packages into "Source-based plugin packages" ("distributed as source code") and "Executable-based plugin packages" ("whose plugin is a pre-built executable"). Its third option, native language packages, is not a Pulumi package, so saying there are two flavors holds. The two differ in how they're distributed and released: source-based packages are distributed from Git and consumed via `pulumi package add` at a Git revision, while executable-based packages ship a binary plus per-language SDKs.
verdicts.framing_note: This is backed only by an editorial sibling docs page; I did not check it against product source.

verdicts.text: Publishing a source-based package to the Pulumi IDP Private Registry is a two-step flow (apply a semver Git tag, then run `pulumi package publish`), typically performed by a CI/CD pipeline that runs on tag.
verdicts.evidence: The cited anchor confirms only the publish step: "Pulumi Cloud customers can publish versions of the package to the Pulumi IDP Private Registry using `pulumi package publish`". The tag-first order is in a sibling guide's CI/CD example: "git tag v1.0.0 / git push origin v1.0.0 / # Publish to Pulumi IDP Private Registry (optional) / pulumi package publish github.com/myorg/my-component@1.0.0".
verdicts.framing_note: The cited anchor doesn't mention a Git tag or running on tag. Those parts are backed only by the sibling guide's pipeline example (other Pulumi docs), not by CLI source. The GitHub code search hit its rate limit.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim calls the tag a required step, but the docs only show it in an example. Whether `pulumi package publish` actually needs a semver tag on the repo hasn't been checked against product source.

verdicts.text: Publishing a source-based package to the Private Registry requires applying a semver Git tag (e.g., `v1.2.3`) to the repository.
verdicts.evidence: The Private Registry docs back this up: "Pulumi uses git tags for versioning components... The tag must adhere to the semantic versioning standard plus a 'v' prefix (e.g. `v1.2.3`)". The troubleshooting table lists "`error: no version tag found`" with the fix "Tag your repository with a semver tag". A GitHub rate limit blocked the check against product source.
verdicts.framing_note: This rests only on a same-site docs page. The pulumi CLI package publish source was not checked.

verdicts.text: `pulumi package publish` sends the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and places the package in the Private Registry.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference, which is transcribed from pulumi/pulumi source, says: "This command publishes a package to the Private Registry. The package can be a provider or a schema." The Private Registry is hosted in Pulumi Cloud, so saying the command sends metadata to Pulumi Cloud is a reasonable paraphrase.
verdicts.framing_note: Source says "Publish a package to the Private Registry"; the claim says it "sends the package metadata to Pulumi Cloud and places the package in the Private Registry". Same meaning, reworded.

verdicts.text: Semver-tagged releases are only required for publishing to the Private Registry; source-based packages referenced directly from a `Pulumi.yaml` file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version.
verdicts.evidence: I couldn't confirm this. The sibling docs only show tag-based refs: source-based-plugin.md L522 has "pulumi package add <repo_url>[/path/to/component]@<release-version>", and L525 says "omit the <release-version> portion" for self-hosted Git servers. They never say branches or non-semver commits work. My searches of pulumi/pulumi source (the git plugin version/ref resolution) hit the GitHub rate limit or came back empty, so I couldn't check the branch/commit/non-semver behavior.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit)" is a broad claim. Pulumi's plugin version resolution is semver-oriented, and non-semver refs may be handled only as commit-hash pseudo-versions, so branch support needs checking against pulumi/pulumi's workspace plugin code.

verdicts.text: Source-based packages referenced directly from a Pulumi.yaml file can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated `pulumi package add` help text (transcribed from pulumi/pulumi source) says Git-repo packages accept a version that "can either be a tag (in semver format), or a Git commit hash." That covers commits, but it doesn't list branches or non-semver tags, so "any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version" claims more than the CLI documents.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Pulumi.yaml `packages` entries use the same repo@version syntax as `package add`. Check the Git ref resolver in pulumi/pulumi (couldn't reach GitHub, rate-limited) before merging.

verdicts.text: Executable-based package releases are produced by a CI/CD pipeline that builds the plugin, generates the SDKs, and pushes everything to the relevant feeds.
verdicts.evidence: This describes the usual release process, and it matches what Pulumi ships: the official provider template repo, pulumi/pulumi-provider-boilerplate, includes CI release workflows (`.github/workflows/release.yml`, `prerelease.yml`, `build.yml`). The sibling packaging-components.md page also says executable packages are "usually distributed as pre-built per-language SDKs published to multiple package managers... with the plugin executable published to an accessible location." I hit a rate limit before I could read inside release.yml, so the build, SDK-generation and publish steps themselves weren't checked.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The sentence says releases always go through CI/CD, but that's the recommended practice, not a requirement; a manual release is also possible. Adding "typically" would make it accurate.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud customers can additionally publish an executable-based package to the Private Registry via `pulumi package publish`.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference (built from pulumi/pulumi source) says: "This command publishes a package to the Private Registry. The package can be a provider or a schema... When <provider> is specified as a local path, Pulumi executes the provider binary to extract its package schema." So `pulumi package publish` does accept executable-based (binary) packages. One caveat: the Private Registry page lists the Enterprise or Business Critical plan as a prerequisite, so the claim's "Pulumi Cloud customers" is broader than the plans that actually have access.
verdicts.framing_note: CLI help says publish accepts a provider plugin reference or a local provider binary, which matches the claim. "Pulumi Cloud customers" is looser than "Enterprise or Business Critical plan".
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Pulumi Cloud customers" may suggest every Cloud tier can use this; the Private Registry is gated to Enterprise/Business Critical.

verdicts.text: An executable-based plugin package is distributed as a pre-built plugin binary, typically alongside per-language SDKs published to package feeds (npm, PyPI, NuGet, Maven, the Go module proxy, or private equivalents).
verdicts.evidence: The anchor #executable-based-plugin-packages exists on the linked page, which says: "Executable-based plugin packages are usually distributed as pre-built per-language SDKs published to multiple package managers (one per consumer language), with the plugin executable published to an accessible location." That matches the claim that the package is a pre-built binary "typically alongside" per-language SDKs. The same page also says pre-publishing SDKs "isn't strictly required".
verdicts.framing_note: Source says "usually distributed as pre-built per-language SDKs ... with the plugin executable published"; the claim says "pre-built plugin binary, typically alongside per-language SDKs". Same meaning. The claim's specific list of package feeds is extra detail and matches ecosystem practice.

verdicts.text: In both source-based and executable-based cases, the released artifact is a single, semantically-versioned Pulumi package.
verdicts.evidence: This is a summary sentence the guide writes about its own subsections (L17–28). I couldn't check it against product source because GitHub code search hit a rate limit (HTTP 403). The same page also partly undercuts it: L24 says source-based packages referenced from `Pulumi.yaml` "can use any Git ref (tag, branch, or commit), regardless of whether it is a valid semantic version." So "semantically-versioned" only holds for packages published to the Private Registry.
verdicts.source: repo:content/docs/iac/guides/building-extending/packages/repository-strategy.md L24, L30; gh search code attempt (rate-limited)
verdicts.intuition_flag: "In both cases ... semantically-versioned" leaves out the qualifier from L24 that semver tags are required only for Private Registry publishing. The page reads as inconsistent with itself.

verdicts.text: A repository containing multiple packages must either release them in lockstep (forcing unrelated work to share a version) or invent per-package release tooling that fights the way Pulumi naturally consumes packages.
verdicts.evidence: L34 is the reasoning behind Pulumi's own recommendation ("A repository should contain exactly one Pulumi package"). It's a trade-off argument ("forcing unrelated work to share a version", "fights the way Pulumi naturally consumes packages"), not a checkable statement about product behavior. The same page (L19–21) bases it on "The package's version is the Git tag on that repository."
verdicts.intuition_flag: If Pulumi supports subdirectory-prefixed Git tags for source-based packages (e.g. `subdir/v1.2.3`, like Go modules), then "invent per-package release tooling" overstates the cost. I couldn't check this because the GitHub search was rate-limited.

verdicts.text: A 1:1 repository-to-package mapping keeps git tags, release artifacts, and version history aligned.
verdicts.evidence: L34 is the reason given for Pulumi's own "one repository per package" recommendation: "A 1:1 repository-to-package mapping keeps git tags, release artifacts, and version history aligned." It's a general engineering point (one repo means one tag and version stream) that backs a best-practice recommendation, not a checkable statement about how the product behaves.

verdicts.text: Multiple components inside a single Pulumi package are supported and expected, and the components ship together at the package's version.
verdicts.evidence: A sibling guide says: "A single plugin package can expose **multiple components**; you do not need one package per component." It also shows the SDK API `componentProviderHost({ components: [StaticSite, Database], name: "my-package" })`. A package has a single version (its Git tag or binary version), so its components ship together at that version.
verdicts.framing_note: Supported only by another Pulumi docs page, which shows the SDK's componentProviderHost API. I couldn't read the SDK source because GitHub returned a rate-limit error, so confidence is medium.

verdicts.text: A single `PulumiPlugin.yaml` file at the repository root defines the package, with components living alongside it (e.g., in a `components/` directory).
verdicts.evidence: The PulumiPlugin.yaml reference says to "Place it at the root of a component package's source directory to declare the authoring language so Pulumi can load the plugin and introspect its components." That matches a single root manifest defining a package that holds several components. The exact `components/` subdirectory is only an example layout. Whether each language's discovery finds components in that subfolder isn't confirmed by this source.
verdicts.framing_note: The reference says the manifest goes 'at the root of a component package's source directory'. The claim is the special case where the repo root is the package root, with components in a subdirectory.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The corroborating source is a same-site reference page, not product source. Per-language component discovery from a nested `components/` dir (e.g., Python __main__.py / TS entry) could be checked in pulumi/pulumi.

verdicts.text: The example repository layout places PulumiPlugin.yaml at the repo root and components under a components/ directory (components/EksCluster/, components/EksIam/) as a valid single-package layout.
verdicts.evidence: The source-based plugin guide describes one `PulumiPlugin.yaml` at the plugin root, an entry file, and component classes that can live in subdirectories (e.g. Python `my_components/components.py`, Go `provider/my_component.go`). It also says "A single plugin package can expose **multiple components**." So a root manifest with a components/ directory works as a single-package layout, as long as the entry file (hidden in the example's "...") exports or registers the components.
verdicts.framing_note: This is an illustrative layout. It is only valid if the entry file (implied by "...") exports the components. For Go, each component must also be listed explicitly in WithComponents.

verdicts.text: When unrelated components share a package, every release of the package versions every component the same way, regardless of whether each component changed, which violates semver.
verdicts.evidence: This is Pulumi's own design guidance, not a checkable product fact. The factual part is consistent with the page's own premise at L11 ("the components inside it inherit the package's version"): components share their package's version. "Violates semver" is the author's editorial judgment explaining why Pulumi recommends against the pattern.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Strictly speaking, semver versions a package's public API as a whole, so bumping to v2.0.0 for ComponentB's breaking change is valid semver. The pattern weakens the per-component signal but doesn't technically violate semver, so the wording may be worth softening.

verdicts.text: In a package with two unrelated components, an enhancement to ComponentA releases the package at v1.1.0 and a subsequent breaking change to ComponentB releases the package at v2.0.0, per semver conventions (minor bump for feature, major bump for breaking change).
verdicts.evidence: (re-verified after own-file-only) L75-79 walk through a made-up sequence ("Consider this sequence with two unrelated components, `ComponentA` and `ComponentB`"). The v1.0.0/v1.1.0/v2.0.0 numbers belong to that invented package. They don't pin any real release, so there's no latest version to check them against. The versioning rule the example uses, a minor bump for a new feature and a major bump for a breaking change, is standard semver and the example applies it correctly.
verdicts.framing_note: Made-up example versions, not real release pins. The only general point is the semver bump rule, which the example applies correctly.
